chapter_en: The Laws of Guarding One's Life

sections.body_en:
It is a Torah mitzva to build a guardrail for the roof of a dwelling house that is used, in order to prevent the danger of falling from it, as it is said (Devarim 22:8): "When you build a new house, you shall make a guardrail for your roof, so that you do not bring blood upon your house if anyone falls from it." And in the Sages' midrash in the Sifrei they learned from the verse that the mitzva of building the guardrail is made up of two mitzvot: a positive mitzva to build the guardrail, as it is said, "you shall make a guardrail for your roof," and a negative mitzva, which establishes that as long as he has left the house without a guardrail, not only has he neglected a mitzva, but he transgresses a Torah prohibition by this, as it is said, "so that you do not bring blood upon your house." And so the Shulḥan Arukh ruled (ḤM 427:6), that whoever leaves his roof without a guardrail has neglected a positive mitzva and transgressed a negative one.

The Rambam wrote (Laws of Blessings 11:12) that when he builds a guardrail for his roof he should bless: "Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us to make a guardrail." And when a Jewish worker builds a guardrail for his fellow, he should bless: "who has sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us concerning the making of a guardrail."

Admittedly, one of the Rishonim, the author of Sefer Ha-Roke'aḥ, wrote that one does not make a blessing over making a guardrail. Perhaps his reason is that the main point here is the negative mitzva – "so that you do not bring blood upon your house" – and one does not bless over a negative mitzva. But in the view of all the other Rishonim one should bless, because the foundation of the mitzva rests on the positive mitzva of "you shall make a guardrail for your roof," and, as is known, before every positive mitzva one should make a blessing.[1]

notes_en.en: So wrote Beit Barukh part 2, Kuntres Ha-Mezuza note 2, in the name of many poskim. And so ruled the Ben Ish Ḥai, second year, Pinḥas 4. And some have the practice not to bless; see Yalkut Yosef, Berakhot p. 601.

sections.body_en:
In the Responsa Ḥatam Sofer (OḤ 52) he wrote that one should make the blessing over the guardrail before finishing building it. The height of the guardrail must be at least ten tefaḥim, and if he built slightly less than this he has not fulfilled the mitzva; therefore only before he finishes building the tenth tefaḥ should he bless. But in the view of all the other poskim, one blesses immediately at the start of building the guardrail, because all the building belongs to the mitzva. And if he forgot to bless at the beginning, he may bless before the end, for as long as he has not yet finished building the guardrail he is still fulfilling the mitzva and can still bless.

It should be added that there is a fundamental dispute about the blessing of "Sheheḥeyanu". In the view of the Tosafot (Sukka 46b), one blesses "who has given us life, sustained us and brought us to this time" only over mitzvot that have a fixed time, and therefore one does not bless "Sheheḥeyanu" over building the guardrail. But in the view of the Rambam (Laws of Blessings 11:9), over every mitzva that is a possession of the person, such as tzitzit or tefillin, one should bless "Sheheḥeyanu", and therefore one should bless "Sheheḥeyanu" also over building a guardrail. And since there is a doubt here, one does not bless "Sheheḥeyanu", because we hold the rule that in a doubt about blessings, one is lenient.

But one who wishes to beautify the mitzvot and merit the blessing may take a new fruit and bless "Sheheḥeyanu" over it, intending by this also the building of the guardrail; and after eating the fruit he should bless over making the guardrail and begin to build it. Or he may buy a new garment and put it on before building the guardrail, and bless "Sheheḥeyanu" over it, intending also the building of the guardrail.

As stated above, the Sages established that the height of the guardrail that the Torah obligated us to build at the edges of high places, such as a roof or a balcony, must be at least ten tefaḥim. This is because only a guardrail ten tefaḥim high gives us reasonable security against falling. However, because of the length of the exile and its wanderings, a dispute arose among the great Aḥaronim as to the measure of a tefaḥ. In the view of most poskim the measure of a tefaḥ is eight centimetres, but some said that the measure of a tefaḥ is ten centimetres. If so, regarding the guardrail, in the view of most poskim a guardrail of eighty centimetres is enough. But in the view of the stringent, among them the author of the Ḥazon Ish, the height of the guardrail must be a full metre.

This guardrail must be strong enough that a person can lean on it and not fall (SA ḤM 427:7), for only such a guardrail can prevent the danger of falling from the roof. Moreover, a guardrail that an adult cannot lean on securely does more harm than good, because a person who does not know that the guardrail is weak may lean on it and fall. Therefore one must take care that the guardrail be strong, and under no circumstances fall when people lean on it.

For the same reason the Sages said that a person is forbidden to keep a rickety ladder in his house, because people will err and think it is strong, and when they climb it they may fall and be hurt (Bava Kamma 15b). And likewise it is forbidden to keep in the house a faulty electrical appliance that may endanger the life of the person using it. And if he was negligent and left a faulty appliance or a rickety ladder for the use of his household, even if nothing happened, he has transgressed the prohibition of "so that you do not bring blood upon your house" (Devarim 22:8).

For all the mitzvot of the Torah we have a rule: "It is a greater mitzva to do it oneself than through one's agent," that is, best of all is for the person himself to fulfil the mitzva. Regarding a guardrail this means that the owner of the house should build the guardrail for his roof, and before that make the blessing "to make a guardrail".

However, many times the owner of the house does not know how to build the guardrail professionally, and he has to take a skilled worker. In such a case, if a Jewish worker builds the guardrail, the owner of the house does indeed fulfil the mitzva, since the worker works as his agent; but he has lost the blessing of the mitzva, because the worker who builds the guardrail is the one who must make the blessing "concerning the making of a guardrail".

And if the owner of the house nevertheless wishes to merit the blessing, he should ask the worker to show him how to build, and before he begins building he should bless "to make a guardrail", build a little, and afterwards the worker continues building the guardrail. In this way the owner of the house can take part himself in the work of building, and by this he can also make the blessing. But as stated, even where the worker builds it all and blesses himself, the owner of the house thereby fulfils the mitzva of building the guardrail.

But if the worker is not Jewish, in the view of most poskim (Rabbi Akiva Eiger, Minḥat Ḥinukh and Maharit Algazi), the owner of the house does not fulfil the mitzva. Rather, after the gentile finishes building the guardrail, the Jew will no longer have a mitzva to build a guardrail for his roof, and he will not transgress the prohibition of "so that you do not bring blood upon your house," since in fact there will be a guardrail on his roof. But the mitzva of building a guardrail he has not fulfilled, because it is not possible to appoint a person who is not Jewish as an agent for mitzvot that only Jews are commanded in. Therefore one who wishes to fulfil the mitzva of building the guardrail in his house must take care to employ a Jewish worker.

Not every roof requires a guardrail. And although it is said in the Torah (Devarim 22:8), "you shall make a guardrail for your roof," nevertheless from the continuation of the verse, "so that you do not bring blood upon your house if anyone falls from it," one can learn that only for a roof that people regularly go up onto, and from which there is a danger that they will fall, is there a mitzva to build a guardrail. Therefore sloping tiled roofs, which are not fit for any use, are exempt from a guardrail. Admittedly, sometimes a worker goes up on them to repair the solar water heater or the tiles there, but these cases are rare, and for them the Torah did not require building a guardrail for the roof, just as a person who must climb a tree or a pole for his work need not first build a guardrail around the place to which he must climb.

And even if the roof is flat, if there are no stairs by which one can go up to the roof, it is exempt from a guardrail, because this roof was not intended for people's use. Only a roof that one can easily go up to must be surrounded with a guardrail, because over the many times, there is a concern lest someone fall from it.

There are people who surround their roof with a kind of low guardrail at the height of a bench, so that one can sit on it. It is clear that this bench cannot be considered a guardrail, and one must build beyond it another guardrail of concrete or iron, which will be at least ten tefaḥim higher than the height of the bench. For there is a concern that children or even adults will climb and stand on this bench-guardrail and fall from the roof, and therefore the guardrail must be built beyond that bench, to a height of about a metre above it (the book "Ve-Asita Ma'akeh" p. 16).

Since people generally use the roof of a dwelling house, and not the roof of a synagogue or beit midrash, or the roof of a cattle shed or a storehouse, therefore, even if it is possible to go up on their roof, there is no mitzva to build a guardrail for it (SA ḤM 427:1-3). And if there is a building which, although it does not serve as a dwelling house, people regularly go up onto its roof, the poskim disagreed as to whether one must make a guardrail for it. For perhaps, since people do not usually go up on the roof of such buildings, those who go up there are careful and there is no need to make a guardrail for them; and perhaps, since in practice people regularly go up on the roof of this building, one should build a guardrail for it. And since there is a doubt in this, one should build a guardrail there without a blessing.[2]

notes_en.en: From the Rambam, Laws of the Murderer 11:1, and SA ḤM 427:1, it is implied that even if people sometimes go up there, they are exempt from a guardrail. And it can be explained (according to what is brought in the Sma 427:2, and Ḥazon Ish ḤM Likkutim 18) that in essence the roof is not so dangerous, because the one who goes up onto it knows that he must be careful, just as it is permitted to climb a tree and to build roofs; but in a place where people commonly go up, namely above a dwelling house, the Torah commanded to build a guardrail. And one can say that since people regularly use them, there is a concern that without noticing they will walk on the roof and fall. But in a place where people do not go up so regularly, those who go up are accustomed to be careful. By contrast, according to the Sifrei brought in the Kesef Mishneh there, one must build a guardrail for them. And so wrote the Smag, positive commandments 77, the Yere'im and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam. Therefore, if people regularly go up there, one must build a guardrail without a blessing. In addition, one can say that even if it is obligatory to build a guardrail, since this is not "your roof", the mitzva is to build a guardrail only in order to remove a hazard, and one does not bless over that.

sections.title_en: 6. Other Places That Require a Guardrail
sections.body_en:
A pit or a well in a courtyard that is ten tefaḥim deep, whether or not there is water in it, requires that a guardrail ten tefaḥim high be built around it, or that it be covered (SA ḤM 427:7). But one does not bless over making the guardrail or the cover for the pit, because the blessing was instituted for the positive mitzva "you shall make a guardrail for your roof," whereas here, where it is not a roof, one fulfils only the negative mitzva – "so that you do not bring blood upon your house" – and no blessing was instituted for a negative mitzva (Ḥayei Adam 15:24).[3]

And likewise in a two-level courtyard, where the difference in height between the two levels is more than eighty centimetres, one must build a guardrail, to prevent falling from the upper level to the lower. And one does not bless over making it. The height of the guardrail must be at least eighty centimetres ("Ve-Asita Ma'akeh" pp. 17-19).

The poskim disagreed as to whether one must build a guardrail for a ramp or stairs that are ten tefaḥim (80 cm) above the ground. Some say that a person is careful when he walks on a ramp or on stairs, and therefore, just as no guardrail was made for the ramp by which they went up to the altar, so there is no need to build a guardrail for a ramp or stairs (Hagahot Maimoniyot, Laws of the Murderer 11:2, based on the Sifrei, and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam). And some say that the ramp by which they went up to the altar was wide, but for an ordinary ramp, and likewise for stairs, if they are ten tefaḥim above the ground, one must build a guardrail for them (Sedei Ḥemed; Ḥayei Adam 15:23). And to get out of a doubt of danger, one should build a guardrail without a blessing.

A road in the public domain beside which there is a private courtyard ten tefaḥim lower than the public domain – the owner of the private courtyard need not build a guardrail there so that those walking in the public domain will not fall into his courtyard (SA 427:4). And the people who walk in the public domain are also not obligated to build a guardrail there, because it is not possible to impose on an unorganised public the building of a guardrail (Sma there 427:8). Nevertheless it is fitting that the heads of the community build a guardrail there. But there is no clear obligation in this, because when the place is wide there is no concern that people will fall, since people do not walk at the edge of the roads.

But when the concern of danger is tangible – whether because the road is not wide, or those walking on it are many, or the drop there is deep, or there is a slope there that increases the risk, or for any other reason – the community leaders are obligated to build a guardrail there. And likewise the Sages said that when there is a need, roads are repaired even on Ḥol Ha-Mo'ed, so that there will be no obstacles in them over which people could stumble. And if they did not do so, then all the blood that was shed there, Scripture regards it as though they had shed it. And Rabbeinu Ḥananel explained that they learned this from the mitzva of the guardrail (Mo'ed Katan 5a).

notes_en.en: In the view of the Smag, positive commandments 77, and the Smak, mitzva 152, it is enough to surround the pit with a fence of three tefaḥim (24 cm). But according to the Rambam a fence of ten tefaḥim is needed, and so is the halakha, as ruled in SA ḤM 427:7. As for the blessing, according to the Gra one blesses over making a guardrail for a pit, but according to the Ḥayei Adam and the Ben Ish Ḥai one does not bless.

sections.title_en: 7. A Mitzva to Remove Dangers and Avoid Them
sections.body_en:
The Rambam wrote (Laws of the Murderer 11:4): "Any obstacle that involves danger to life, it is a positive mitzva to remove it and to guard against it and to be very careful in the matter, as it is said (Devarim 4:9): 'Take heed to yourself and guard your soul diligently.' And if he did not remove it, and left the obstacles that lead to danger, he has neglected a positive mitzva and transgressed 'you shall not bring blood.'"

And although the verse "take heed to yourself and guard your soul diligently" (Devarim 4:9) warns mainly not to forget the gathering at Mount Sinai, nevertheless the Sages learned from it that one must also guard one's life (Berakhot 32b, and see Shevu'ot 36a). That is, the verse comes to warn each and every one of Israel to guard his life from destruction; and just as one who forgets the gathering at Mount Sinai loses his soul, so too one who puts himself in danger loses his life, so that he cannot continue to engage in Torah and the service of Hashem.

Therefore a person is forbidden to raise a vicious dog and let it roam unchained. And even if the dog is not accustomed to bite but only barks and frightens, lest it frighten a pregnant woman and cause her to miscarry. And the Sages said of one who raises a vicious dog, that is, a frightening dog, and does not chain it, that he is cursed. But in settlements near the border it is permitted to raise a vicious dog, so that it will guard against enemies; and by day they should chain it and by night release it (Bava Kamma 83a; SA ḤM 409:3). And a dog that does not bark and frighten may be raised anywhere, and there is no need at all to chain it (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Laws of Guarding the Body and Soul 3).

And likewise a person is forbidden to keep a rickety ladder in his house, lest someone who does not know that the ladder is rickety come there, climb it and fall (Bava Kamma 46a).

And a person should not walk under a leaning wall that may fall, nor walk on a rickety bridge, lest it fall just as he crosses there (see Rosh Ha-Shana 16b, Ta'anit 20b).

And it is forbidden to leave a poisonous substance in a place where small children can reach it and eat or drink from it. And likewise it is forbidden to leave a poisonous substance, such as bleach, in a bottle that people drink from, lest someone come who does not know that a poisonous substance was put in the bottle, and drink from it and die.

And likewise it is forbidden to leave in the house a faulty electrical appliance by which the user may be electrocuted.

Likewise it is forbidden to go on a dangerous hike. And there are two levels of danger. There are routes that are truly dangerous, and even for trade people do not travel them; on these it is forbidden to hike because of danger to life. And there are routes that involve a little danger, and people travel them for trade and livelihood; but for a hike, intended for pleasure and amusement, it is fitting not to go on them. And who determines what a dangerous route is? People who have experience, such as officials in charge of this in the police, or people responsible for rescue units.[4]

notes_en.en:
The distinction between livelihood and a hike is explained in Igrot Ha-Re'aya part 3, p. 132. And likewise we find that people climb scaffolding to build houses, and poles to install electricity lines and change lamps, and although there is danger in this, the needs of livelihood and subsistence, even for the sake of greater comfort, are important needs, and it is permitted to take a slight risk for them. In addition, the workers who engage in this know from their experience to be more careful. But for play and pleasure one should not enter these dangers.
And see the article of Rabbi Yehuda Amiḥai (Emunat Itekha 18), who explained that there are two levels of danger: when the danger is tangible, the prohibition of endangering oneself is Torah law, and about this the Rambam wrote in Laws of the Murderer 11:4, and the SA copied it in ḤM 427:8; and in a remote concern the prohibition is rabbinic, and about this the Rambam wrote there in halakha 5, and the SA in se'if 9; see there. And it seems to me that what our master Rav Kook wrote, "that it is not fitting", refers to things in which even the Sages did not establish a prohibition, but there is in them a remote concern of danger, and therefore it is not fitting to go out to them for pleasure. And see Igrot Moshe OḤ 2:59 (s.v. 'u-meduyak') that there is no prohibition in this. It must further be said that even in things that are forbidden rabbinically, for a real need it is permitted, and therefore it is permitted to climb poles in order to repair something at their top.

sections.body_en:
Question: Many ask: what is the attitude of halakha to smoking cigarettes or a pipe – is it permitted to smoke or forbidden?

Answer: Hundreds of years ago, doctors thought that smoking was beneficial to health, and sometimes they would recommend to certain patients to smoke a pipe as a remedy. Apparently smoking does indeed help stimulate digestive activity, and perhaps some other positive things, and therefore the doctors thought that smoking was beneficial to health. But over time it became clearer and clearer that, taken as a whole, smoking is very harmful to health.

Already in the period of the Ḥafetz Ḥayim, the opinion of several doctors became known, who held that a weak person is forbidden to get used to smoking, because smoking weakens his strength and may even cause his death. And on this basis the Ḥafetz Ḥayim determined, nearly a hundred years ago, that a person is forbidden to accustom himself to smoke.

Even so, since it was not clear how harmful smoking is, most rabbis held that there was no absolute prohibition in this, only a recommendation. Therefore they did not protest against the yeshiva students who were in the habit of smoking.

But over the last decades it has become clear beyond a shadow of doubt, on the basis of thorough studies, that smoking is very dangerous to health; and if so, it is clear that there is a Torah prohibition against smoking. For the Torah commanded us to guard our lives, as it is said (Devarim 4:9): "Only take heed to yourself and guard your soul diligently," and likewise it is said (there 4:15): "Take good heed of your souls." And likewise the Torah commanded us to beware of anything that may endanger life, as it commanded us to make a guardrail for the roof. From all this we learn how much a person is commanded to guard his life and his health, and it follows that it is clear that smoking is forbidden by Torah law (Aseh Lekha Rav part 2, 1; Tzitz Eliezer 15:39).

Incidentally, it is worth noting here that Rabbi Dr. Mordechai Halperin wrote that it is possible that the prohibition of smoking derives not only from the mitzva to guard one's health, but even from the prohibition of murder. For with every inhalation of smoke into the lungs, the smoker causes direct damage to his lungs, and to a certain extent brings his end closer, and thus he transgresses the severe prohibition "You shall not murder" mentioned in the Ten Commandments.

It is also forbidden to smoke a nargila, for various studies have proven that nargila smoke contains various dangerous toxins that may cause cancer and heart disease. Admittedly, there are not yet clear studies of how many die from this, but it is agreed that there is a risk in smoking a nargila.

Let us briefly review the scientific facts, as they are brought in the book Assia (part 5, pp. 222-237, the articles of Dr. Meltzer, Dr. Hershkowitz and Prof. Katan), which served as the basis for the halakhic ruling forbidding smoking.

Three main kinds of disease are caused by smoking. The first is direct damage to the lungs, through bronchitis and emphysema. These diseases damage the defence mechanisms in the lungs that are meant to protect against the entry of harmful agents into the body, and likewise damage the lungs' ability to absorb oxygen. In most cases these diseases damage physical fitness and the ability to function, and in rare cases these diseases cause death. The second kind is heart disease: roughly one of every four people who die of a heart attack dies because of smoking. And the third kind is cancer. In comprehensive surveys it has been proven that smoking is the main environmental factor in the development of cancer. The risk that a man who smokes will develop cancer is twice as high as for a man who does not smoke. Smoking causes mainly lung cancer, to the point that among smokers the chance of developing lung cancer is seven times higher than among those who do not smoke. According to the statistical calculation, it was found that every year (around the year 5750) more than five hundred people in the country die of lung cancer because of smoking.

In general summary, it emerges that the death rate among smokers is much higher than among those who do not smoke. For example, in a huge survey by the insurance companies in America, it was found that the death rate among men smokers aged forty-five is 80% higher than the death rate among men of their age who do not smoke. And among sixty-year-olds, the death rate among smokers is 125% higher than among those who do not smoke.

In an interesting study by one of the insurance companies, it was found that the rate of road accidents among smokers is also higher than among those who do not smoke. 6.59% of smokers were involved in road accidents, whereas among those who do not smoke only 3.75% were involved in road accidents. The reason for this is that smoke damages the haemoglobin, and thereby the amount of oxygen in the blood decreases, which causes damage to the driver's ability to concentrate and judge.

Following these studies, many insurance companies raised the price of the policy for smokers.

And for our purposes, on the basis of all the above data, it has been ruled in halakha that there is a severe Torah prohibition against smoking.

sections.title_en: 10. The Prohibition of Smoking Near Others
sections.body_en:
A halakhic question concerning the problem of smoking is whether a person can demand of his fellow that he stop smoking, because the smoke disturbs him. It is clear to all that in a private home the authority to decide whether to smoke or not lies in the hands of the owner of the house. Therefore a guest cannot oblige the host to stop smoking. And likewise a guest cannot smoke against the wishes of the owner of the house.

The question is what the law is in public places, or in places that belong to several people: can one who does not want people to smoke near him demand of his neighbours that they stop smoking or not?

In the Talmud (Bava Batra 23a) it is explained that even in his private domain, a person must take care not to create damage to his fellow. For example, a person is forbidden to create in his domain a bad smell or smoke that will penetrate his fellow's domain and harm him. And from here there is clear proof that smoke is defined in halakha as something harmful and disturbing, and that a neighbour can demand of his fellow not to create smoke that will reach his domain and distress him. And so is the law in a public place: a person can demand of his neighbour that he stop smoking. And likewise two clerks working in an office – one clerk can oblige his fellow to stop smoking in his vicinity.

And even if for a long time the neighbour kept silent and did not protest against the smoker, nevertheless he has not lost his right, and whenever he protests against his fellow, the fellow will be obligated to stop smoking. And even if the smoker claims that he has been smoking here for many years, and until now no one asked him to stop, and therefore he has a ḥazaka and a right to continue in his habit, nevertheless according to halakha one can demand of him to stop smoking. For it is known that smoke greatly disturbs those who suffer from it, and a person cannot claim that he has a ḥazaka and a right to do something that harms his neighbours (SA ḤM 155:41).

And all this was said even when it was not known that smoke is harmful to health, and they knew only that it causes distress to the one who smells it. But today, when it is known that smoke also harms those who are near smokers, the prohibition is much more severe. For example, it has become clear in studies that when one spouse smokes, the other spouse's chances of developing cancer are three times higher than those of a person whose spouse does not smoke.

And so my teacher and master Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda Ha-Kohen Kook ztz"l, head of the Merkaz Ha-Rav yeshiva, instructed that one should not smoke in the beit midrash. And as we have learned, even before the clear studies on the dangers of smoking were published, there were rabbis such as the Ḥafetz Ḥayim who opposed smoking for moral reasons, among them: needless addiction, disturbance to neighbours who suffer from the smoke, neglect of Torah study and waste of money. And this was the position of my teacher and master Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda Ha-Kohen Kook ztz"l. And indeed in the Merkaz Ha-Rav yeshiva there were almost no smokers, and with Hashem's help the good custom spread from it to all the other yeshivot that follow the light of our master Rav Kook ztz"l.[5]

notes_en.en:
In the old age of my teacher Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda, at a time when he no longer came to the yeshiva frequently, he was told that there were a few who smoked in the library or in the beit midrash, and in the days of Seliḥot of the year 5737 he wrote a call to stop smoking. And because of the endearing quality of his words I will bring his letter, which from then until today hangs at the entrance of the beit midrash of the Merkaz Ha-Rav yeshiva: "To all our brothers and friends in the beit midrash and in the library. The great and forceful request and demand, in the very holy days of these Seliḥot and repentance, in the strength of their completeness between a person and the Omnipresent and between a person and his fellow, to wean oneself and refrain entirely from the habit of smoking and sucking pieces of the tobacco plant in the mouth and the lips, which in our happiness are sanctified to the toil of the glory of the Torah and the attachment of its fellowship.
Happy is he who hastens and strengthens himself to do this, to increase the force of diligence in Torah and its purity, and abundance of contentment for the friends and the strength of their diligence and pleasantness. Torah scholars in the Land of Israel are called 'pleasant', because they are pleasant to one another in halakhot and in conduct, pleasantness in the ways and peace in the paths, and thereby abundant strengthening and mutual success in establishing learning and making it strong, with the appearance of help from Heaven for the sanctification of Hashem and the merit of the many.
Yours faithfully, with great love and everlasting love, Tzvi Yehuda Ha-Kohen Kook."
A few years later, in the year 5744, smoking was also forbidden absolutely in the hall of the Ponevezh yeshiva, by the instruction of the head of the yeshiva, Rabbi Shach ztz"l. And likewise Rabbi Feinstein ruled that it is forbidden to smoke in a beit midrash or in a synagogue, because the smoke harms the neighbours (Assia 5, p. 248).

sections.title_en: 11. Is It Permitted to Help a Smoker Buy Cigarettes?
sections.body_en:
One of the first rabbis who, in the light of the scientific studies, published the halakha that smoking is forbidden was Rabbi Ḥayim David Ha-Levi ztz"l, the chief rabbi of Tel Aviv.

And a further question came before him: is it permitted to help a person who smokes? For example, a father who asks his son to buy him a packet of cigarettes – is he permitted to buy it or forbidden? On the one hand, we have learned that there is a Torah prohibition against smoking cigarettes, because it is harmful to health, and it is forbidden to help in a transgression. And on the other hand, there is a mitzva to honour father and mother.

And Rabbi Ḥayim David Ha-Levi answered that since it has been ruled that honouring parents does not override the mitzvot of the Torah, the son is forbidden to comply with the father's request and buy cigarettes for him. Admittedly there is no Torah prohibition in this of "you shall not put a stumbling block before the blind," because the Torah prohibition applies only where without the help the transgression would not have been carried out, and here the father can get cigarettes even without the son. Nevertheless there is a prohibition of the Sages here, since they said that even when a person can commit the transgression without help, his fellow is forbidden to help him in a transgression. Therefore the son is forbidden to buy his father the cigarettes, because this is helping in a transgression (Aseh Lekha Rav 6:58).

In principle he is right, but if this would cause a great quarrel, it would turn out that in the end the son would cause serious damage to the relationship of love and honour that ought to exist between him and his father, and his gain would be outweighed by his loss. Therefore it seems that where refraining from buying cigarettes would not be understood by the father, and it would cause tension and distress in the family, it is better that the son buy his father the cigarettes, and thereby prevent damage to the relationship between him and his father.[6]

notes_en.en: Similarly, Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach wrote (Minḥat Shlomo part 1, 35:1) that one should not refrain from offering refreshments to someone who will not make a blessing over them, because not offering the refreshment would cause a more severe transgression, of hatred, than the transgression that would be caused if he gave him food and he did not bless. End of quote. And indeed it seems that if the smoking would cause an imminent danger to life, it would be forbidden to give it to him, as the Beit Leḥem Yehuda and the Birkei Yosef YD 240:15 wrote. But here the danger is not imminent. And it seems to my humble opinion that the harm caused by cigarettes differs from person to person, and on the other hand stopping smoking may sometimes cause psychological harm, which indirectly may also cause danger. Therefore, although one should make great efforts to stop smoking, one should not do it with too heavy a hand. Therefore too one should not cause a great quarrel with one's parents over it. But if the son can say that he does not want to be a partner to this, and his father will understand him, even with difficulty, all the better. But if this would cause great tension, it is better that he buy him the cigarettes.

sections.title_en: 12. Is It Permitted to Advertise Cigarettes in a Newspaper?
sections.body_en:
Question: The cigarette companies invest large sums in advertising. In the newspaper "Be-Sheva" too, the cigarette companies asked to advertise themselves with a large investment. Is there any permission to advertise cigarettes? It should be added that the law obliges advertisers to state that cigarettes are harmful to health; does this addition permit the advertising?

Answer: Since we have learned that smoking is dangerous to health, it is forbidden to cause people to stumble and to encourage them to smoke, as it is said (Vayikra 19:14): "You shall not put a stumbling block before the blind." There are two stumbling blocks here: the very encouragement to endanger oneself, which is truly a stumbling block before the blind; and in addition, the advertising causes people to stumble into transgressing the Torah prohibition of endangering life.

And one cannot claim that advertising does not cause people to smoke, for if so, why would the cigarette manufacturers be prepared to invest huge sums in advertising, just to support the newspapers? It is clear that advertising encourages smoking, and most serious of all, that it entices young people to enter the circle of smokers. And this is perhaps its main aim: to cause young people to become addicted, and to ensure the continuation of their profits. And this is truly the Torah prohibition "you shall not put a stumbling block before the blind."

Nor can one claim that if they do not advertise in the newspaper "Be-Sheva", they will find other places to advertise, because every advertisement in a further media outlet increases the influence of the advertising. Moreover, since the other media outlets too belong to Jews, they too consequently transgress a Torah prohibition, and therefore there is no argument that if we do not sin, others will sin in our place (as in the words of the Mishneh La-Melekh and the Ḥavvot Da'at YD 160, brought in the Pitḥei Teshuva YD 160:1). On the contrary, it is our duty to protest against this, as it is said (Vayikra 19:17): "You shall surely rebuke your fellow" (as explained in the Bi'ur Halakha 608:1). Therefore one must protest against the newspapers called "Ḥaredi" that advertise cigarettes and transgress a Torah prohibition.

Now that we have learned that there is a Torah prohibition against smoking, because smoking causes damage to health and endangers the life of the smoker and those around him, one must demand of every person that he not begin to smoke cigarettes or a pipe. For before a person has become used to smoking, he can easily refrain from it, but after he has become addicted to the habit and to nicotine – it is very hard to stop.

Even so, one who is already used to smoking cigarettes also bears a Torah mitzva to stop smoking. And indeed, after stopping smoking, the risk of developing heart disease or cancer gradually decreases, until after ten years the chance of developing heart disease is similar to the chance of any person who did not smoke. And the increased risk of developing cancer disappears after fifteen years (Assia part 5, p. 224 and p. 235).

Admittedly, at first glance it seems that it is very hard to stop smoking, but experience shows that through explanation and education even one who is used to smoking can stop. For example, in the year 5730, when studies about the danger of smoking began to be published, 64% of doctors were in the habit of smoking. And when they were asked whether in their opinion it was possible to stop smoking, they thought not. But ten years later, only 16% of doctors continued to smoke. The conclusion from this is that a clear recognition of the danger posed by smoking helps very much in stopping smoking. Therefore smokers have a duty to learn about the dangers of smoking, and to do everything in order to stop smoking.

It is true that sometimes a person's psychological state, or the environmental pressures he is under, hardly allow him to cope with the task of stopping smoking, and then perhaps he can be defined as acting under compulsion. And sometimes it is advisable to suggest to such a person not to try to cope with stopping smoking, because this struggle may disrupt his psychological balance and perhaps thereby cause a health risk. But the great majority of people are able to cope with stopping smoking.

Incidentally, it is worth noting that smoking also causes the loss of a great deal of money. A person who smokes for fifty years, two packets of ordinary cigarettes every day, pays for them close to one hundred and fifty thousand shekels. And if he had saved that same money and accumulated returns on it as is usual in savings plans, he would have more than three hundred thousand shekels at the age of seventy.

Question: What is the attitude of halakha to insurance? Is it right for a person to insure himself with life insurance, or insurance against fire and damage or injury, in order thereby to provide for his future and his family? Or perhaps there is in this a lack of faith in Hashem, for if the Holy One, blessed be He, wills, all will be well, with no untimely death and no mishaps and damage. And more than that: even if, Heaven forbid, the family's breadwinner dies before his time, if Hashem wills, he will succeed in leaving a substantial inheritance to his family; whereas if Hashem does not will it, the insurance too will not help. If so, the question is whether there is not in life insurance a lack of faith in Hashem?

Answer: Rabbi Feinstein wrote (Igrot Moshe OḤ 4:111) that there is no lack of faith whatsoever in buying an insurance policy, because it is like all the business a person does.

And in every business one must take into account all the considerations and the risks, and one does not rely on a miracle; rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, runs the world in the way of nature. And just as a person cannot say, "I will not go to work, and if Hashem wills He will send me a livelihood, and if He does not will it then even if I work I will have no livelihood," so a person cannot say, "I will not insure myself, and if Hashem wills nothing will happen to me." Rather, the natural risks exist and one must deal with them in natural ways. And therefore Rabbi Feinstein concludes that it is good and fitting even for upright and God-fearing people to insure themselves.

That is: faith does not say, do nothing and rely on Hashem; rather, do everything that is needed according to reason and according to nature, and know that even after you have done the most, you still need Hashem's help.

And in this is revealed, in essence, the role of man to be a partner with the Holy One, blessed be He, in the repair of the world. The person exerts himself and strives for the sake of Heaven, and Hashem is the one who gives the strength and the assent for his efforts to bear fruit. And if he does not thank Hashem, then he denies His help, as it is said (Devarim 8:17-18): "But you shall remember the Lord your God, for it is He who gives you strength to make wealth." And if he relies on a miracle, he betrays his role, as it is said (Devarim 14:29): "So that the Lord your God may bless you in all the work of your hand that you do."
